examGuide.title: Mental model and derivation
examGuide.body:
Binary heaps combine complete shape with parent-child ordering. Sibling order is unrestricted. One-based indices give parent floor(i/2), children 2i and 2i+1. Bottom-up build-heap is linear because most nodes are near leaves; multiplying n by worst-case sift height overestimates it. A min-heap gives constant root lookup, but extracting the minimum restores order and takes logarithmic worst-case time.

**Key relationship:** Zero-based children of i: 2i+1 and 2i+2; parent=floor((i−1)/2)

examGuide.title: A repeatable solving procedure
examGuide.body:
1. Use a fixed index convention.
2. Separate shape from heap order.
3. Trace swaps and charge work by node height.

examGuide.title: Approach the exam question
examGuide.body: For a one-based heap, children are 2i,2i+1 and leaves start at floor(n/2)+1. Heap order compares ancestors and descendants, not siblings. Bottom-up build-heap is linear even though one sift can be logarithmic. In a distinct-key min-heap the maximum must be a leaf.

examGuide.title: Worked problem
examGuide.body:
How many leaf positions exist in a binary heap with 100 elements?

**Answer: 50.** Internal indices are 1 through floor(100/2)=50. Leaves are 51 through 100, giving 50 positions. This follows from completeness and applies to min-heaps and max-heaps.

examGuide.title: Conditions and edge cases
examGuide.body:
Reading the extreme root is O(1); extracting it must restore heap order and can take O(log n).

A min-heap’s inorder traversal is not generally sorted.

examGuide.title: Worked question patterns
examGuide.body:
#### Pattern 1 · MCQ

In a one-based binary heap, parent of index 13 is:

- **A.** 5
- **B.** 6
- **C.** 7
- **D.** 26

**Answer: B.** Parent index=floor(13/2)=6.

#### Pattern 2 · MSQ

Choose true statements.

- **A.** Heap shape is complete
- **B.** Bottom-up build-heap is O(n)
- **C.** A min-heap root contains a minimum key
- **D.** Extract-min may require O(log n) work

**Answer: A, B, C, D.** All statements hold: complete shape, linear build, minimum root and logarithmic worst-case extraction.

#### Pattern 3 · NAT

A binary heap contains 101 elements. How many are leaves?



**Answer: 51.** Internal indices end at floor(101/2)=50. Leaves number 101−50=51.

#### Pattern 4 · NAT · Transfer problem

How many distinct min-heaps can seven distinct keys form in the complete seven-node shape?



**Answer: 80.** The smallest key is root. Choose three of the six remaining keys for the left subtree: 20 choices. Each three-node heap has two orders for its leaves. Product=20·2·2=80.

examGuide.title: Work through the supplied PYQs
examGuide.body:
#### GATE 2025 CS1 · Q35 · NAT

[Open the original question and try it](/#/lesson/binary-heaps?tab=practice)

**What is tested:** Binary heaps and priority queues. Refer to the original image for complete givens and diagrams.

1. A binary heap is a complete binary tree: levels before the last are full. Levels of edge-heights 0 through 4 hold 1+2+4+8+16=31 nodes.
2. The 32nd node occupies level 5, and the height is measured in edges as specified.
3. Height=floor(log₂32)=**5**, independent of min-heap key ordering.

#### GATE 2026 CS1 · Q23 · MSQ

[Open the original question and try it](/#/lesson/binary-heaps?tab=practice)

**What is tested:** Binary heaps and priority queues. Refer to the original image for complete givens and diagrams.

1. With one-based indexing, internal nodes occupy indices 1 through floor(n/2)=(n−1)/2 for odd n. Leaves start at (n+1)/2.
2. Both (n−1)/2 and (n−3)/2 are internal; the n>100 condition keeps these positive. (n+1)/2 and n are leaves.
3. The nonleaf choices are **B,C**.
